findings.summary: The section 1 table's third column overlaps the section 3 "The Subdomain Trap" bullet list, making both unreadable where they collide.
findings.evidence: Table cells reading "Sent to", "app.example.com only", "parent + ALL subdomains", "same, dot is legacy" are printed on top of the bullets "XSS or takeover on blog.example.com reads a Domain= session", "Worse: it can also overwrite that cookie", "Cookie tossing: same name set on the parent shadows the real one", "Host-only is the safer default — widen only when forced"
findings.fix: Constrain the section 1 table to the left column width (drop or wrap the third "Sent to" column) so it does not extend under the right-hand column, and reflow section 3 to start below the table's actual bottom.

findings.summary: The caption promises a session-vs-JWT table and a ship checklist that the part never delivers, ending instead at session auth.
findings.evidence: Caption: "Ends with the session-vs-JWT table and a ship checklist you can paste into your auth PR" — the last slide is "Session Auth", closing on the "Signed Cookie Sessions" callout; no JWT, comparison or checklist page exists.
findings.fix: Either append the Token Auth, Session vs Token and Checklist chapters from the syllabus, or rewrite the caption's last sentence to end at session auth and label the part (e.g. "Part 1 of 2") with the JWT/checklist material promised for the next part.

findings.summary: The whole-jar cookie limit is stated as ~180, which is actually the per-domain limit; the total jar limit is ~3000–3300.
findings.evidence: Table rows: ["Per domain","~50 cookies"], ["Whole jar","~180 cookies"]
findings.fix: Set "Whole jar" to "~3000 (RFC minimum) / 3300 in Chrome" and note that real browsers allow ~180 per domain even though the spec floor is 50.

findings.summary: CSRF is load-bearing from the first page to the end of the part but is never expanded or defined anywhere.
findings.evidence: Page 1: "That automatic-ness is the root of CSRF"; page 5: "CSRF token cookie is the one standard exception"; page 6: "The browser-level CSRF mitigation" — no page states what CSRF is.
findings.fix: Add one bullet under page 1's "State On A Stateless Wire": "CSRF = another site triggers a request to yours and the browser attaches your cookies anyway." Do the same for XSS before page 3's "XSS or takeover on `blog.example.com`".

findings.summary: A whole chapter of Set-Cookie attribute reference is filed under a continuation title from the previous chapter, so it is unfindable by its own subject.
findings.evidence: Page 2 is headed "Why Cookies Exist (cont.)" with `"cont":true`, yet after the three-bullet "What People Store" block it covers "The Full Grammar", "Scope Attributes", "Lifetime Attributes", "Safety Attributes" and "Silent Failure Modes" — the entire "Anatomy of Set-Cookie" chapter.
findings.fix: Move "What People Store" to the end of page 1 and retitle page 2 "Anatomy Of Set-Cookie" with `cont` removed.

findings.summary: "Site" is defined as scheme-less eTLD+1, but Chrome's Schemeful Same-Site (default since Chrome 89) makes the http and https versions cross-site for SameSite purposes.
findings.evidence: "`https://a.example.com` vs `http://b.example.com:8080`" / "Different origins, same site — cookies see one thing"
findings.fix: Distinguish the two senses: cookie storage/scoping ignores scheme and port, but SameSite uses schemeful site (scheme + eTLD+1), so `http://` ↔ `https://` on the same domain is cross-site in Chrome; pick a same-scheme example for "same site".

findings.summary: "Session fixation" is used as the payoff of the cookie-tossing attack four pages before it is defined.
findings.evidence: Page 3: "Cookie tossing: same name set on the parent shadows the real one" / "Shadowed cookie enables session fixation" — the definition arrives only on page 7: "Session fixation: attacker plants an ID, victim logs in, attacker owns the session."
findings.fix: On page 3, replace the bare term with an inline gloss, e.g. "Attacker plants a known ID that the victim then logs in under — session fixation", and keep page 7's fuller treatment as the callback.

findings.summary: The cookie-tossing claim depends on the shadowing/precedence mechanics that are not explained until page 4.
findings.evidence: Page 3 asserts "same name set on the parent shadows the real one" with no account of why the fake wins; page 4 supplies it: "Browser sends both: `Cookie: sid=a; sid=b`" / "Most servers read only the first — shadowing is trivial."
findings.fix: Add one bullet to page 3's "The Subdomain Trap" stating that the browser sends both cookies in one header and most servers read only the first, or move the tossing bullets to page 4 after the send-order rules.

findings.summary: The claim that `Secure` restricts only sending and not writing is obsolete and contradicts the deck's own page 5 callout.
findings.evidence: Page 4: "It restricts SENDING, not writing" vs page 5: "Modern browsers block that — older ones did not."
findings.fix: Replace with "Originally it restricted only sending; since Chrome 52's 'Leave Secure Cookies Alone' (now in RFC 6265bis) a non-secure origin can neither read nor overwrite a `Secure` cookie."

findings.summary: The verification command in the "Verify In The Browser" box runs past the right page edge and is truncated mid-word.
findings.evidence: curl -i https://site/login | grep -i se  — the line ends at the page boundary with "se" clipped (presumably "set-cookie"), and the box's right border is cut off at that row
findings.fix: Wrap the command onto a second line (e.g. break before `| grep`) or shrink the code font so the full `curl -i https://site/login | grep -i set-cookie` fits inside the box.

findings.summary: The `Secure` section is split across a page boundary so page 5 opens with an exception to a rule stated on the previous page under an unrelated title.
findings.evidence: Page 4 (titled "Path, Prefixes, Precedence") ends with heading "Secure: HTTPS Only" … "It restricts SENDING, not writing"; page 5 then opens with callout "The Overwrite Hole" — "Pre-RFC6265bis, plain HTTP could overwrite a `Secure` cookie even without reading it."
findings.fix: Move the "Secure: HTTPS Only" heading and its five bullets from the end of page 4 to the top of page 5, directly above "The Overwrite Hole", so the rule precedes its exception on the same page.

findings.summary: Firefox does not treat an omitted `SameSite` attribute as `Lax` — it still defaults to `None`, so the claim overstates browser-level CSRF protection.
findings.evidence: "Omitted attribute = `Lax` on modern Chrome, Firefox, Edge" / "Older browsers treated the omission as `None`"
findings.fix: Change to "Omitted attribute = `Lax` on Chrome and Edge; Firefox still defaults to `None` (Mozilla bug 1617609 was resolved WONTFIX after the Firefox 96 attempt was reverted for breakage) — always set `SameSite` explicitly."

findings.summary: The caption promises a session-vs-JWT table and a ship checklist that do not appear anywhere in these seven pages.
findings.evidence: "Ends with the session-vs-JWT table and a ship checklist you can paste into your auth PR."
findings.fix: Either add those two blocks to the final page or rewrite the caption's last sentence to describe what the part actually ends with (session store trade-offs and expiry discipline).

findings.summary: `=` inside a cookie value does not break parsing — RFC 6265 splits the pair at the first `=` only.
findings.evidence: "Raw `;` `,` space or `=` in a value breaks parsing"
findings.fix: Drop `=` from that list (base64/JWT values routinely carry `=` padding); keep `;`, `,`, and space.

findings.summary: RFC 6265bis is listed as the current spec, but it is still an Internet-Draft in the RFC Editor queue with no RFC number; RFC 6265 is the published standard.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["Current spec","RFC 6265bis"]
findings.fix: Write "RFC 6265 (2011); RFC 6265bis draft-22 in the RFC Editor queue — already what browsers implement."

findings.summary: The cookie-tossing description says a same-name parent cookie shadows the real one, but send order is by path length then oldest-first creation time, so a later parent cookie at the same path sorts after the legitimate one.
findings.evidence: "Cookie tossing: same name set on the parent shadows the real one" (vs page 4: "Send order: longer `Path` first", "Equal paths tie-break by creation time, oldest first")
findings.fix: State the actual mechanism: the attacker sets the same name with `Domain=example.com` at a *longer* `Path` so it sorts first in the `Cookie` header and the server reads it instead.

findings.summary: The claim that `Path` is not a security boundary rests on an unexplained mechanism while every comparable claim on the page gets a worked example.
findings.evidence: Page 4 callout: "Same-origin JavaScript reads cookies at any path through iframe tricks." The page's other rules each carry a demonstration (`Path=/admin` match list, `Cookie: sid=a; sid=b`, the `__Host-sid` header).
findings.fix: Add a two-line example showing the mechanism — e.g. inject an iframe at the cookie's path and read `iframe.contentDocument.cookie` from the parent — so the reader can see why `Path` isolates nothing.

findings.summary: The "Verify In The Browser" box contains an empty bullet with no text.
findings.evidence: A lone "·" appears on its own line between "Check the browser, not the source code" and the curl command
findings.fix: Attach the curl command to that bullet or remove the empty list item from the box content.

findings.summary: Two named mechanisms in the "Non-Negotiable Set" section are invoked as justification without ever being explained.
findings.evidence: Page 5: "Double-submit needs JS to read it — deliberately non-`HttpOnly`" and "HSTS removes the first plaintext request entirely" — neither "double-submit" nor "HSTS" is defined anywhere in the part.
findings.fix: Expand in place: "double-submit: the same CSRF token is sent in both a cookie and a request field, so JS must read it" and "HSTS (`Strict-Transport-Security`) tells the browser to use HTTPS from the start".

findings.summary: Rails' cookie session store is encrypted and authenticated (AES-256-GCM), not merely HMAC-signed as stated.
findings.evidence: "Rails and Flask style: data lives IN the cookie under an HMAC."
findings.fix: Say "Flask signs the payload with an HMAC; Rails encrypts and authenticates it (AES-256-GCM since 5.2) — either way the data rides in the cookie."
